options.consequence: One diff for shutdown, but 66 of 95 bus-api@v1 cases and 23 of 45 bus-testing@v1 cases call start(), and bus-api@v1 G8, G18 and bus-testing@v1 G5, G9, G14, G17, G18 call shutdown(), so almost no behavior replays before the last phase.

chosen: start with the publish path, shutdown incremental (D8)
why: The suites cannot replay delivery without start(), and several non-lifecycle guarantees assert on shutdown; incremental teardown keeps each slice's shutdown with the code that owns the resource. Recorded as D8. Signal that would change it: a reviewer who wants all of shutdown in one diff.

question: How do gates check bus-api@v1 G38, G39 and bus-testing@v1 G20 ('checked by nidana.runtime's gates'), given that every gate must be an fvm command?

options.label: Package test plus one provider library (D9)
options.consequence: A test in packages/nidana_dart_runtime/test checks the pubspec and the sources; every timer and microtask goes through one internal provider library, so the check can forbid Timer( and the global scheduleMicrotask( elsewhere; the pipeline gets its timer through its port.

options.label: grep in each gate
options.consequence: Not an fvm command, not run with the package's tests.

options.label: Review only
options.consequence: zone.run at each call site cannot be told apart from a timer outside the zone by a source check.

chosen: Package test plus one provider library (D9)
why: ADR-003 Consequences anticipates a source search for DateTime.now(, Stopwatch( and timers outside the provider implementation; a Dart test keeps the gate an fvm command, and model-gate-commands showed fvm dart test packages/{member} runs from the workspace root. Recorded as D9.

question: Is the delivery slice one phase or several?

options.label: Pure core, registry and cells, publish path; ownership separate
options.consequence: Four phases of about 330 to 420 lines each (nidana.runtime.2, .6, .7, .8); .6 replays no guarantee of its own because its cases publish through publishers.

options.label: One delivery phase plus ownership
options.consequence: About 850 lines, two PEs in one review sitting.

chosen: Pure core, registry and cells, publish path; ownership separate
why: The stand-in's registry, cells, publish path, observers and recorder seam are about 400 lines without docs or tests (docs/auto-run/experiments/bus-api-widened/packages/nidana_dart_runtime/lib/src/bus.dart); the PE ceiling forces the split.

question: Is the pipeline one phase or two?

options.label: Two phases
options.consequence: Synchronous stages and sinks first (.9), then switchMap, retry, time stages and cancellation (.10), which need the virtual scheduler.

options.label: One phase
options.consequence: About 750 lines with tests; one review sitting cannot hold it.

chosen: Two phases
why: The stand-in interpreter alone is 438 lines; the split follows ADR-003 items 3 and 4, which govern the second half only.

question: Is activation one phase or two?

options.label: Checks and handles, then wiring
options.consequence: nidana.runtime.11 (planOf, idempotency, limits, analyses, handles, ownership, live graph, activation observers) runs beside the pipeline lane; nidana.runtime.12 implements the port and the connection timing and binds the live suite. Each replays guarantees of its own.

options.label: One activation phase
options.consequence: About 660 lines and 8 or more tasks, above the PE; the connection timing reviewed together with the checks.

chosen: Checks and handles, then wiring
why: Merged it exceeds the PE; the read path's timing (D3) is the seam that moved most in the experiments (D1 point 4), which is a stated reason to review it in isolation. The fixtures confirm the split has replay value: G1, G10, G20, G21, G24, G32, G37 pass without wiring.

question: Where do the small slices go: telemetry (about 100 lines) and the residual lifecycle (startup window, onShutdown, G36 order)?

options.label: Telemetry with test support, lifecycle with module scopes
options.consequence: Two phases of about 330 and 400 lines; each pair is a sizing-floor merge (same tier, no third phase needs one without the other).

options.label: Separate phases
options.consequence: Two phases below the floor whose process artifacts would exceed their diffs.

chosen: Telemetry with test support, lifecycle with module scopes
why: The sizing floor: a phase must earn its cycle; telemetry alone and the residual lifecycle alone do not. Signal that would change it: a separate owner for observability.

question: When does a guarantee join a producing gate's --guarantee list?

options.label: When every case of it can pass
options.consequence: Lists derived case by case from the fixtures; several guarantees replay later than the phase that implements their slice (delivery guarantees from the ownership phase on).

options.label: When its slice lands
options.consequence: Gates would fail: most cases publish through publishers, call start(), or activate a topology.

chosen: When every case of it can pass
why: ADR-001 item 10 restricts behavior to the guarantees delivered so far, and a gate must pass; a case runs only when every id it covers is in the restriction (item 9). The derivation is mechanical and reproducible.

question: How are producing phases' gates written: 'node default plus' the replay, or the full command?

options.label: Full command per producing phase
options.consequence: Each producing phase's Gate is a complete fvm chain; hsdd-config copies it verbatim into the phase context and the superpowers derivative.

options.label: node default plus replay
options.consequence: Shorter, but hsdd-config replaces only a Gate that is exactly 'node default', so the context could carry an unresolved phrase.

chosen: Full command per producing phase
why: hsdd-config's switch rule resolves 'node default' only as the whole Gate value; the full command avoids an implementing session guessing the default.
evidence: .agents/skills/hsdd-config/SKILL.md (The Generic Phase Context, The Superpowers Derivative)

question: How are the pipeline phases verified before activation composes them?

options.label: Unit tests against a port of the test's own
options.consequence: As D2 and the Isolation strategy state; the live suite replays through Bus.activate from the wiring phase on.

options.label: Bind the live suite to a test-local mini bus
options.consequence: Earlier coverage of topology-dsl@v1 G18 to G29, but the harness would re-implement delivery, dedup and reentrancy in test code, about 150 to 200 lines more per phase.

chosen: Unit tests against a port of the test's own
why: D2 already decided it; a test-local bus that passes the live suite is a second runtime to maintain. Signal that would change it: a pipeline defect that the unit tests missed and the live suite caught at the wiring phase.

question: Does the pipeline reuse the delivery core's per-read dedup state, making nidana.runtime.9 depend on nidana.runtime.2?

options.label: Reuse the delivery core's dedup
options.consequence: One implementation for observed subscriptions and topology reads (bus-api@v1 G16, topology-dsl@v1 G19); .9 waits on .2.

options.label: Pipeline's own dedup
options.consequence: .9 depends only on the package; two implementations of one rule.

chosen: Reuse the delivery core's dedup
why: G16 and live G19 state the same rule; one function keeps them from drifting, and .2 is an early pure phase, so the wait is short.

question: Does test support and telemetry (nidana.runtime.13) wait on activation wiring, or run beside it after ownership with a smaller replay?

options.label: Wait on activation wiring
options.consequence: Its gate replays bus-testing@v1 G3, G12 to G19 and bus-api@v1 G33, whose cases activate topologies; serial anyway, since both edit lib/src/bus.dart.

options.label: Run beside activation
options.consequence: Its gate could replay only bus-testing@v1 G15 and G16; the rest would join at a later gate, and the two phases would still serialize on bus.dart.

chosen: Wait on activation wiring
why: The collision on bus.dart (TestBus) serializes them regardless; waiting lets the phase replay what it delivers.

question: Which phases are listed as producing bus-api@v1 and bus-testing@v1?

options.label: Phases that implement public members
options.consequence: bus-api@v1 [.1, .5, .6, .7, .8, .11, .12, .13, .14], bus-testing@v1 [.1, .5, .7, .13, .14]; .6 and .7 produce members whose guarantees replay later; pure and pipeline phases produce none.

options.label: Phases that add a replayed guarantee
options.consequence: Drops .6 and bus-testing's .7, hiding where observe, getCurrentValue and the recorder seam are implemented.

chosen: Phases that implement public members
why: Reconcile writes the Delivery paragraph from the confirms and the gates' lists; naming the implementing phases and saying when their guarantees replay tells consumers both facts.

question: Phase 1 is above the ~400-line PE (about 420 lines). Split it?

options.label: Keep one phase
options.consequence: Gate-only, mostly declarations and doc comments; the replay checks it mechanically.

options.label: Split
options.consequence: ADR-001 item 10 runs surface and reject in full from the first producing phase, so each contract's declarations must land in one phase, and the two contracts share a library (D1 point 1).

chosen: Keep one phase
why: The split is not allowed by ADR-001 item 10; the overage is small and declaration-heavy.

question: Review tiers for the effect phases: full-review throughout, or spot-check for the ownership phase?

options.label: full-review for every effect phase but test support
options.consequence: Ownership (single-writer enforcement), delivery timing, activation and the scheduler are business logic and orchestration; test support and telemetry are well constrained by their suites.

options.label: spot-check for ownership
options.consequence: Lighter review of the claims check, which enforces Spec §3.11 layer 1.

chosen: full-review for every effect phase but test support
why: The skill puts orchestration and business logic at full-review; single-writer enforcement is a guarantee consumers rely on for correctness.

question: amend bus-api@v1 G41's outside clause per D5: can it break a consumer?

options.label: Compatible
options.consequence: The clause stated no behavior for an off-type value; nothing changes for a value of the topic's value type.

options.label: Breaking
options.consequence: Reconcile takes it to the human.

chosen: Compatible
why: It adds behavior where the contract was silent, and no fixture of any contract publishes an off-type value; evidence in docs/auto-run/experiments/off-type-delivery/.

question: amend bus-testing@v1 G16 per D6: can it break a consumer?

options.label: Compatible
options.consequence: Identity holds wherever G16 could hold it; only a widened envelope gets an equal copy where the old wording threw.

options.label: Breaking
options.consequence: Reconcile takes it to the human.

chosen: Compatible
why: Probe P2 showed the earlier wording threw a TypeError for exactly the case that changes; == comparisons hold in both cases.

question: amend bus-testing@v1 G18 per D7: can it break a consumer?

options.label: Compatible
options.consequence: Only calls for one topic at two type arguments change, where the old wording could not hold; one publisher per topic keeps one claim.

options.label: Breaking
options.consequence: Reconcile takes it to the human.

chosen: Compatible
why: T7 in bus-api-widened showed the old wording fails at run time for that case.

question: S30's gates nidana.runtime.5 to .11 assume the replay tool passes bus_activation_test.dart (bus-api@v1's binding of topology-dsl@v1's live suite) when no case of it falls within --guarantee. Does that agree with nidana.model D2, or is it a request-style assumption conflicting with another node's entry (a collision)?

options.label: agree
options.consequence: No collision. D2 item 4 (a slug's behavior cases run only as the restriction admits them; a slug with no id in the restriction runs none of them) and ADR-001 item 9 (a bare G{n} is the replayed slug's; the tool learns a binding's suite from the conformance library it imports; a case runs only when every id it covers is in the restriction) leave the live binding with no admitted case at .5 to .11, and D2 item 1 fails a run only on a failing or PENDING fixture. The two implementation hazards the experiment shows go to the hsdd-adr clarification of ADR-001 item 9 already recommended at S29.

options.label: disagree
options.consequence: A collision: stop before applying anything; the orchestrator would arbitrate between changing nidana.runtime's gates and changing nidana.model's tool semantics.

chosen: agree
why: Both texts make an excluded case not run and neither makes an empty selection a failure or a usage error; nidana.model.6's scope adds 'a slug with no id in the restriction runs no binding'. Read with ADR-001 item 9, the slug that matters for a binding is the slug of the suite it imports (topology-dsl), which has no id at .5 to .11. The experiment found two ways a tool could still fail the gates, neither of which D2 permits: dart test exits 79 ('No tests ran') when the name filter admits nothing (E2), and nidana.runtime.11's bare bus-api ids used as a raw name filter would run topology-dsl's same-numbered live cases G18 to G21, G24 and G29 before the pipeline is wired (E3). The per-binding empty case is implied rather than stated, hence medium confidence. The signal that would have changed my mind: D2 or nidana.model.6 stating that a binding whose filter admits no case is run anyway, or is an error.
evidence: hsdd/spec/nidana.model.md D2 items 1 and 4, nidana.model.6 Scope

question: bus-testing@v1's consumers frontmatter is [nidana.navigation, nidana.flutter, nidana.integration], while nidana.runtime's Contracts table (S26 finding) and S30's confirm sub-bullet name nidana.tooling as a contract-edge consumer. Add nidana.tooling now, or wait for its plan's confirm?

options.label: wait for its confirm entry
options.consequence: The frontmatter stays one consumer short until nidana.tooling.lint's plan is reconciled; the Delivery paragraph already names nidana.tooling's edge; no reconcile writes a consumer no plan emitted (S29's precedent for topology-ir@v1).

options.label: add nidana.tooling now
options.consequence: Matches the spec tables at once, but writes a consumers entry no pending section carries, outside step 4's rule.

chosen: wait for its confirm entry
why: hsdd-reconcile step 4 applies confirm entries only, and the consumer is nidana.tooling.lint, whose plan will confirm phase ids. phase_ids stays provisional either way.

question: How do nidana.runtime's consumer confirms land in the three model contracts' consumers lists: replace the node id with the confirmed phase ids, or keep the node id?

options.label: replace the node id with its phase ids
options.consequence: consumers lists nidana.runtime.1 to .14 as confirmed (13, 6 and 3 ids) beside the unplanned node ids; the registry's consumer count becomes 17, 10 and 5 entries, not nodes.

options.label: keep the node id
options.consequence: The registry count stays a node count, but the confirm is not applied and hsdd-contract's gate 'consumers lists phase ids that actually consume this contract' fails for a planned consumer.

chosen: replace the node id with its phase ids
why: hsdd-contract's quality gate asks for phase ids, the step prompt says the contracts gain nidana.runtime's consumer phase ids, and produced_by already carries phase ids since S29. The count change in INDEX.md is derived data.

question: The three behavioral amends (bus-api@v1 G41 off-type clause, bus-testing@v1 G16, bus-testing@v1 G18) add behavior their existing cases do not reach. Cover them with new cases in this edit, or apply the body changes with not-executable lines and schedule an hsdd-contract step?

options.label: five new cases now
options.consequence: Three G41 cases (observed subscriptions, conversions at a call with the reduceInto seed and activate's rollback, topology reads at connection and later delivery), one G16 case, one G18 case; checked against a stand-in patched for D5 to D7, against the unpatched stand-in and against seeded defects; no follow-up step.

options.label: not-executable lines and an hsdd-contract step
options.consequence: Faster here, but a behavior that can be executed is recorded as not executable until a later step adds the cases.

chosen: five new cases now
why: The step prompt prefers fixtures when the work is a few cases, and the stand-in of docs/auto-run/experiments/bus-api-widened/ needed a patch of four small hunks. Results: every suite that imports nidana_dart_runtime passes on the patched stand-in (bus-api 98/98, live 43/43, bus-testing 47/47, navigation 40/40 and 52/52, flutter-binding 52/52 and 26/26); on the unpatched stand-in exactly four of the five new cases fail (the observed-subscription case passes there, since that stand-in already converted in the subscriber's callback); five seeded defects each fail the case of what they break; both structure prototypes pass. No reject fixture changed, so no reject code needed confirming. The new cases join the --guarantee lists S30 already scheduled (G41 at nidana.runtime.12, G16 and G18 at nidana.runtime.13).

question: The G41 amend makes getCurrentValue and getBufferedValues throw TypeError at the call for an off-type value, while G8 says 'neither throws except TopicCollision'. Is the amend still compatible, and what happens to G8?

options.label: compatible; G8 names the TypeError
options.consequence: G41 gains the off-type clause and G8 reads 'neither throws except TopicCollision, or the TypeError G41 states for a value that is not of the topic's value type'; v1 kept with a Versioning line.

options.label: breaking; stop for the owner
options.consequence: The run stops until the orchestrator decides whether to bump bus-api to v2 or drop the amend.

options.label: apply G41 only
options.consequence: The contract reads as self-contradictory between G8 and G41.

chosen: compatible; G8 names the TypeError
why: Before the amend no behavior conformed to G8 for an off-type current value: G8 also says getCurrentValue is the last value delivered, which is not of the type the call returns, and topic-model@v1 offers generic code no way to check a value against a topic's type at publish (nidana.runtime D4, D5), so an implementation could only throw or return a value G8 does not allow. No consumer can have relied on a no-throw result. flutter-binding@v1 G5 builds from getCurrentValue but states nothing for an off-type value, and no fixture of any contract publishes one. A careful engineer might still have shown the owner the G8 edit, since it touches a throw statement the Breaking list names. The signal that would have changed my mind: a consumer contract or fixture expecting a fallback value for an off-type current value.

question: The amend entry says each conversion runs 'in the delivery callback of the one subscription or topology read it serves' and lists the conversions made at a call. A read's connection is converted during activate. Does the G41 text say which rule covers it?

options.label: state the connection explicitly
options.consequence: G41 says 'its first values and a read's connection included'; an off-type connection value goes to the provider zone's handler and activate returns normally; case three pins it.

options.label: keep the entry's wording
options.consequence: A reader could take the connection for a conversion made during activate and expect activate to throw, which nidana.runtime.12's scope does not do.

chosen: state the connection explicitly
why: D4 has every topology read convert each payload and nidana.runtime.12's scope converts 'each value' in the read's own callback, connection values included; only the reduceInto seed throws to the caller. Saying so removes the one ambiguity a consumer could build on. The signal that would have changed my mind: a plan text that throws from activate for an off-type connection value.
evidence: hsdd/spec/nidana.runtime.md D3, D4, D5, nidana.runtime.12 Scope

question: In the Delivery paragraphs, does 'phase X delivers G{n}' name the phase whose gate first replays the guarantee or the phase that implements its slice?

options.label: the phase that first replays it
options.consequence: Consumers wait for a guarantee whose cases pass at a producing gate; nidana.runtime.6 (registry, cells, observed streams) and nidana.runtime.7 (bus-testing@v1's recorder seam) are named as implementing phases whose guarantees replay later.

options.label: the phase that implements its slice
options.consequence: Earlier dates, but a consumer could build on a guarantee no gate has checked yet.

chosen: the phase that first replays it
why: The conventions' Contracts paragraph reads delivery from the plan's entries and its gates' --guarantee lists, and S30's confirm sub-bullets list the replay phases, naming .6 and .7 separately. The paragraphs also carry note 4: G38, G39 and bus-testing@v1 G20 are checked by packages/nidana_dart_runtime/test/package_properties_test.dart, because the not-executable line format ('checked by {node}'s gates') is ADR-001's and parsed by the structure set.

question: topology-dsl@v1's Delivery paragraph says G18 to G29 'are the live implementation's'. Does it gain the phase that delivers them, which S30's topology-dsl confirm sub-bullet states (replayed from nidana.runtime.12 on)?

options.label: add the phase
options.consequence: Consumers of topology-dsl@v1's live semantics (navigation, flutter, integration) read that nidana.runtime implements them and that they replay from nidana.runtime.12, pointing at bus-api@v1's Delivery.

options.label: leave the paragraph
options.consequence: Those consumers would have to find the date in bus-api@v1, a contract some of them do not consume through a contract edge.

chosen: add the phase
why: The convention puts which producing phase delivers which guarantees in the contract a consumer reads; for G18 to G29 the producing node is nidana.runtime, not the produced_by nidana.model phases. One clause, no guarantee changes.

question: The drained entries resolve no OQ, but two citations of OQ-R1 (RESOLVED 2026-10-17 by bus-api@v1 G17) still read as open: ADR-003 item 6 'whichever first-delivery timing OQ-R1 gives', and nidana.flutter's 'a new observe subscription may receive its first value one microtask later'. Sweep them now?

options.label: sweep both
options.consequence: Both cite bus-api@v1 G17 as the resolution and state the timing; no decision, item or link changes; the quality gate 'no artifact still cites a resolved OQ as open' holds.

options.label: leave them
options.consequence: The sweep stays limited to OQs this drain resolves, and the two stale citations survive until another reconcile or the owners' next touch.

chosen: sweep both
why: OQ-R1 belongs to the node being drained, the skill's quality gate is tree-wide, and the step allows an ADR edit for step 13's citation sweep. S29 swept ADR-003's OQ-M3 line the same way, without an Amendments entry.

question: note 1 (nidana.runtime.1 is the node's only member-creating phase; the conventions' 'one phase each of nidana.runtime' is nidana.runtime.1): does it change a convention?

options.label: no change
options.consequence: The Shared workspace files bullet stays as written; the rule already covers nidana.runtime.1, and the plan's scope carries the phase id.

options.label: name nidana.runtime.1 in the bullet
options.consequence: The bullet names a planned phase for the runtime as it does for nidana.model, but reconcile writes a plan fact into the conventions without a rule change.

chosen: no change
why: hsdd-reconcile step 10 applies a note only when it changes a convention and drops derived facts; the note confirms the plan follows the rule. Notes 2 (replay sets used) and 3 (empty selection) change no convention either: note 2 restates the Phase design bullet, and note 3 is tool behavior that ADR-001 item 9 and nidana.model D2 own. The signal that would have changed my mind: an executor of another node needing the runtime's member-creating phase id and having no other place to read it.

question: While applying the G41 amend, S31 edited bus-api@v1 G8 ('neither throws except TopicCollision') so it also names G41's TypeError for an off-type value, and flagged it as a possible breaking amend. Is it the breaking-amend run-stop?

options.label: Not a stop; keep the edit
options.consequence: G8 and G41 agree; the stand-in experiment shows every suite that imports nidana_dart_runtime still passes.

options.label: Stop the run
options.consequence: The owner decides a wording change to a guarantee that no implementation could meet as written.

chosen: Not a stop; keep the edit
why: The breaking-amend stop guards an existing consumer. No consumer code exists, and before the edit G8 could not be satisfied for an off-type value at all, because G41 already required the TypeError; the edit removes a contradiction rather than taking a promise away. Every consuming contract's fixtures pass against the amended stand-in (docs/auto-run/experiments/runtime-reconcile-amends/).

question: navigation-api@v1 G13 fixes the nav-resolver's edges and order but not the functions they record; topology-ir@v1 G9 leaves a closure anonymous. Should the template's two stage functions be closures or named method tear-offs?

options.label: method tear-offs of private stage classes
options.consequence: The recorded IR and every rendered graph name the stages resolveDeepLinks and applyAuthGuard, as Guide §3.4 draws them; about 35 more lines; consumers can see the names, so a compatible amend of G13 goes to reconcile and hsdd-contract adds an assertion or a not-executable line.

options.label: closures
options.consequence: No extra code and no amend, but two of the resolver's three transforms render as (anonymous) in bus.toGraph(), the catalog and the JSON form.

chosen: method tear-offs of private stage classes
why: Spec §6.2 asks for named transformers and Spec §6.5 treats a topology as self-documenting data; the experiment shows tear-offs record the names in both forms, keep two resolvers of one configuration equal, and pass all 40 navigation cases and 52 executor registrations unchanged. Because the names are visible across the boundary the choice is emitted as an amend rather than kept node-local.

question: How to cut nidana.navigation into phases under fp-progression: where the resolver template and resultsFor go, and whether the in-memory router stands alone.

options.label: six phases, template with the guard
options.consequence: Declarations; values; access, guard and resolver template (full-review, ~400 lines); executor values and planner; in-memory router; executor and live wiring. The security chain (guard table plus resolve-before-guard order) is reviewed in one sitting; the guard work waits on nidana.model.11 for its G13 replay.

options.label: seven phases, template in its own phase
options.consequence: A spot-check template phase of about 180 lines that could run beside the values and planner lanes as soon as nidana.model.11 merges; one more cycle whose process artifacts would rival its diff, and the guard and the stage order reviewed apart.

options.label: five phases, router folded into the planner
options.consequence: One cycle fewer, but the merged phase comes to about 500 lines, over the review window, and mixes the pure band with the effect band.

chosen: six phases, template with the guard
why: The template alone sits below the sizing floor, and the guard and the template's stage order together are one security property (navigation-api@v1 Refinement 3), so reviewing them together in one full-review phase buys more than the parallel lane. resultsFor rides with the template because both are recorded DSL compositions. The signal that would have favored seven phases: nidana.model.11 expected to land much later than nidana.model.8, holding up the guard work.

question: Review tier of nidana.navigation.3 (access values, resolveDeepLinks, applyAuthGuard, navResolver, resultsFor), a mostly pure phase.

options.label: full-review
options.consequence: A full design and verification doc and a diff read for a pure phase; the guard table and the stage order get edge-case review.

options.label: spot-check
options.consequence: Cheaper review of well-constrained pure functions with exhaustive fixture cases; a subtle guard or order error relies on the fixtures alone.

chosen: full-review
why: The phase decides access: an error in G12's table or in the template's stage order opens a protected route, the bypass navigation-api@v1 Refinement 3 exists to close. The tier table puts security at full-review.

question: Where do the live resolver replays (G14, G16) land: with the resolver template, or in the final phase with the executor?

options.label: final phase
options.consequence: The template phase stays pure and waits on nothing later than nidana.model.11; G14 and G16 replay once, at nidana.navigation.6, which waits on nidana.runtime.14 anyway.

options.label: with the template
options.consequence: The template phase would wait on nidana.runtime.14, the hard edge, putting a pure phase on the critical path after the runtime ships.

chosen: final phase
why: --guarantee selects by guarantee id, and G16 has one recorded and one live case, so G16 cannot replay before a real TestBus exists; G14 is all live. The template adds no code for live behavior, which is the runtime's interpretation of the recorded plan. Keeping nidana.navigation.1 to .5 off nidana.runtime.14 lets them merge while the runtime's later phases run.
evidence: ADR-001 item 9 (--guarantee restricts behavior cases by name prefix)

question: Which phase replays G9 (the five topic declarations, complete at nidana.navigation.1), whose case needs topic-model@v1's values from nidana.model.8?

options.label: nidana.navigation.3
options.consequence: nidana.navigation.2 starts after nidana.model.6 alone; nidana.navigation.3 already needs nidana.model.8 for G13's TopicRef comparisons.

options.label: nidana.navigation.2
options.consequence: The topics replay one phase earlier, but nidana.navigation.2 and everything after it wait on nidana.model.8.

chosen: nidana.navigation.3
why: It removes a cross-node wait from nidana.navigation.2 at no cost, since nidana.navigation.3 depends on nidana.model.8 for G13 regardless.
evidence: topic-model@v1 Delivery (nidana.model.8 delivers every behavior guarantee)

question: Should the executor and the live composition (G14, G15, G16, G24 and the bootstrap test) be one phase or two?

options.label: one phase
options.consequence: About 360 lines (100 of library code), 7 plan tasks, full-review; nidana.flutter's binding of the executor suite waits on one phase.

options.label: two phases
options.consequence: An executor phase and a live-wiring phase that writes almost no library code; the second's process artifacts would exceed its diff, and flutter's G24 replay would wait on a later phase than G18 to G23.

question: How much does the amendment say about the library key: only that it differs between JIT and AOT (S33's finding), or what the key depends on?

chosen: what the key depends on, as measured
why: Ten minutes of code settled it: the same library's key is @22518013 under `dart run` and `dart test`, @21518013 under the Flutter tester, @18518013 under AOT, @28518013 when six libraries are imported ahead of it and @22518013 when the same six come after it; another URL changes the last six digits. question: Does the private-name row need a behavior case, and if so what does it assert?

options.label: no case
options.consequence: G9 keeps its two cases, which test public names only; a FunctionRef.of that strips the key violates G9's rule and the new row yet passes every case (S6 shows it does today)

options.label: a case pinning the JIT key
options.consequence: asserts e.g. `_privateTwice@NNNNNNNN`; the value moves with the conformance library's imports, the test runner and the SDK, so the case would fail on changes that break nothing

options.label: a case asserting the @ and a key, never the value
options.consequence: asserts the name matches `^_privateTwice@.+$` and `^_reduceQuietly@.+$`, equals itself within the process, and is unequal to `FunctionRef.named('_privateTwice')`; stable across programs and runners; fails only if the producer strips or drops the key, or if a future SDK stops rendering the key, which would also make the row wrong

chosen: a case asserting the @ and a key, never the value
why: It closes a real coverage gap in G9 (a stripping or anonymizing FunctionRef.of now fails this case and nothing else, S5) without pinning a process-dependent number. Its one dependency on the VM's rendering is of the same kind as the existing G9 case asserting 'buildCheckoutUi', so it adds no new class of SDK sensitivity. A signal that would have changed my mind: a consumer binding this suite under a runner that is not the VM.

question: Where does the new text go: one table row, or a row plus a paragraph?

options.label: row plus a Private names paragraph
options.consequence: the row shows what each private form renders per compiler; the paragraph states what the key depends on, the consequence for definitions, graphs and graph documents, the cross-references, and that it adds no guarantee

chosen: row plus a Private names paragraph
why: The step asked for the row and the consequence; the consequence is a sentence, not a cell. The row covers every private form the probe measured (top-level, static, instance method, named constructor of a public class, constructor of a private class) so no reader has to extrapolate, and the obfuscated and web cells come from the same probe.

question: G9's gloss reads 'which on the VM is the name of a top-level function, a static method without its class, or a method tear-off', inexact for a private name; and the paragraph after the table says the catalog runs 'where names are as written'. Edit either?

options.label: leave G9 and the sentence verbatim
options.consequence: smallest diff; the new case still traces to G9's rule, but two sentences of the contract stay inexact for private names, which is what this consistency pass exists to fix

options.label: add a clause to G9's gloss and say 'public names'

chosen: add a clause to G9's gloss and say 'public names'
why: Both sentences describe what the rule yields; the rule already yields the key, so the edits narrow nothing and oblige the producer to nothing new. Leaving them would make the new case look as if it tested something G9 does not say. The step framed the change as a statement of existing behavior, and the Versioning line records it as such.

question: Does the contract say what the key looks like, so a tool can compare up to it, as topic-codegen@v1 allows?

options.label: say nothing about its form
options.consequence: topic-codegen@v1's 'compares up to that key' stays undefined for a tool author

options.label: state its form as observed
options.consequence: 'The key is `@` followed by digits; outside an obfuscated build, removing each key gives the name as written', with a measured example; a descriptive line under the table's 'on the pinned SDK', not a guarantee, and the case does not assert digits

question: Decide how a subscriber's error reaches the listen zone while item 6 still holds (everything a `bus.observe` subscription schedules is delivered by the scheduler operations), for example by keeping the callbacks in the provider zone and forwarding each error to the listen zone's handler, or by binding the callbacks to the listen zone.

options.label: Callbacks in the provider zone, errors forwarded to the listen zone
options.consequence: Item 2 keeps where callbacks run and where the bus subscribes. A Timer a callback creates and the timer of a debounceTime chained onto the observed stream stay virtual on a TestBus listened from a test body (C7, C8, T3, T4 pass). Callbacks still do not see the listener's zone values and read the provider clock. The bus wraps every handler, including ones set later through StreamSubscription, in a guard: about 8 ns per delivery per subscriber (C14).

options.label: Callbacks bound to the listen zone
options.consequence: Errors and zone values follow the subscriber, as on any Dart stream. But a Timer a callback creates and the timers RxDart operators chained onto the observed stream create during delivery run on the listen zone's timers: on a TestBus listened from a test body advanceTimeBy fires none of them (C7, C8; T3 and T4 fail), the loss ADR-003 already rejected 'bus.observe returning the subject's stream unchanged' for. Same cost as forwarding.

options.label: Errors stay in the provider zone, as first accepted
options.consequence: Contradicts Spec §10.2 principle 5. Under package:test with a TestBus built in setUpAll, the test whose subscriber threw passes and the runner reports the error against setUpAll, after it completed (T2).

chosen: Callbacks in the provider zone, errors forwarded to the listen zone
why: Spec §10.2 principle 5 fixes where a subscriber's exception goes (the zone in which listen was called), not where its callbacks run; both forwarding and binding satisfy it, measured (C3 to C6, C10, T2). Only forwarding keeps the virtual-time property item 2 was chosen for: under binding, timers a callback or a chained operator creates during delivery leave the scheduler (T3, T4 fail), the same loss for which ADR-003 already rejected returning the subject's stream unchanged. The two cost the same (C14). The signal that would have changed my mind: a consumer that needs its own zone values inside its callbacks, such as package:test's addTearDown or expectAsync called from a callback, or a zone-scoped logging context, which binding gives and forwarding does not.

question: Spec §10.2 principle 5 names an exception thrown by a callback. Do an error event the subscriber leaves without an onError handler (such as TopicRemoved, bus-api@v1 G9), and an exception thrown by a handler set after listen through StreamSubscription.onData/onError/onDone, follow the same rule?

options.label: All of them go to the listen zone
options.consequence: One rule for everything a subscriber leaves unhandled, matching Dart's convention that an unhandled error event goes to the subscription's zone, which for an ordinary stream is the listen zone, and Stream.cast's handling of a failed cast (C12). The runtime's subscription wrapper must wrap handlers set later too (C6).

options.label: Callback exceptions only; unhandled error events to the provider zone
options.consequence: A subscriber that listens without onError, in a test body, would not fail its test on TopicRemoved; two destinations for one subscriber's unhandled errors.

chosen: All of them go to the listen zone
why: A subscriber's unhandled error is the subscriber's, whether it is thrown by its callback or is an error event it chose not to handle; Dart sends both to the subscription's zone, and the experiment shows the wrapper reaches all four paths (C3 to C6). No evidence suggests a consumer wants the provider zone for error events.

question: Does ADR-003 decide whether a conversion at a subscription's own type argument (bus-api@v1 G41, widened references) counts as the subscriber's callback, whose error goes to the listen zone, or as the bus's own delivery code, which Spec §10.2 says is a defect and is not swallowed?

options.label: Leave it to bus-api@v1 (handoff H3)
options.consequence: ADR-003 states only that the bus catches what a subscriber's callbacks throw and that its own delivery code is not caught by that rule; bus-api@v1 states the conversion. The Consequences say bus-api@v1 states it.

options.label: Decide it in ADR-003
options.consequence: ADR-003 would rule on widened references, which are bus-api@v1's subject and not the time source's; the intake record (L4, 'Left to decide') and H3's prompt item (4) give this to H3.

chosen: Leave it to bus-api@v1 (handoff H3)
why: The intake record routes the question to H3, and it concerns G41's widened references rather than zones or time. ADR-003 supplies the rule H3 builds on and the measured precedent (C12: Dart's Stream.cast sends a failed cast to the listen zone's handler, or to onError when one is given).

question: Restate item 6's first-delivery sentence for Spec §2.1 'Replay timing' and §3.13: does ADR-003 fix when a subscription connected at start() receives its first values?

options.label: State the invariant, leave the start() timing to bus-api@v1
options.consequence: Item 6 says a bootstrap topology or subscription is connected at start() and receives its first values within start() or in provider-zone work start() schedules; a subscription after start() gets its replay in the first provider-zone microtask after listen. Either timing H3 picks keeps item 6.

options.label: Fix the first values synchronously inside start()
options.consequence: Pre-empts H3's design of the barrier machinery (Guide §6.1: bus-owned storage and fan-out or a wrapped subject).

options.label: Fix the first values in a provider-zone microtask after start()
options.consequence: Same pre-emption, and a bootstrap subscription would see its replay after start() returns, which H3 may not want for Spec §3.13 step 2's ordering.

chosen: State the invariant, leave the start() timing to bus-api@v1
why: Item 6 needs only that the first delivery is a bus operation or provider-zone work, so that scheduler operations deliver it; the barrier's connection order and timing are bus-api@v1's guarantee (H3). The handoff's sentence is stated as given.

question: Amend in place with a dated `## Amendments` entry, keeping the status, date and item numbers; supersede ADR-003 only if item 2 or item 6 is replaced as a whole, and record why.

options.label: Amend in place
options.consequence: status accepted, date 2026-10-17 and items 1 to 9 kept; a 2026-10-20 Amendments entry records what changed; every Governed by link stays valid.

options.label: Supersede with ADR-004
options.consequence: A new file, ADR-003 set superseded, every Governed by link and affects list moved, for a change to one bullet of item 2 and one of item 6.

chosen: Amend in place
why: Neither item is replaced as a whole: item 2 changes where a subscriber's error goes, not where callbacks run or where the bus subscribes, and item 6 keeps its rule that scheduler operations alone deliver everything a TestBus schedules (C1, C2, T1 measure it under the chosen rule). Item 5's guarded-run bullet gained one clause and keeps its meaning for work that reaches the scheduler.

question: Spec §10.2 principle 5 and Guide §6.1 say which zone a Dart subscriber's error goes to but not which zone its callbacks run in. Mark that for upstreaming?

options.label: Mark it for upstreaming
options.consequence: ADR-003's upstream bullet gains it; the Specification's 'context where the subscriber subscribed' could otherwise be read as the zone callbacks run in (binding), which loses virtual time for another Dart implementation.

options.label: No mark
options.consequence: The Specification is satisfied as written; the reading stays an implementation detail of this tree.

chosen: Mark it for upstreaming
why: The Specification is consistent with the decision, so nothing is resolved against it; but the gap admits a reading the experiment shows breaks Spec §3.6's determinism on a TestBus, and a Guide §6.1 sentence would close it. Weak signal: no other Dart implementation is known to read it otherwise.

question: decide how a `reduceInto` sink maps to a write chain

options.label: One write chain per reduceInto
options.consequence: Its fold and the stages that feed its events form one chain: a reducer that throws, or an error that reaches the sink, ends it and cancels the events stages that feed no other live chain; the state topic keeps its value. Matches Spec Appendix A.1, which defines reduceInto as a scan seeded with the topic's current value, so a reduceInto is a write of a scan.

options.label: A reducer error skips the event and the fold goes on
options.consequence: Treats the reducer unlike every other transformer; contradicts Spec §10.2 principle 4 (transformers must not throw; a throw ends the chain) and v1 G26's 'a reducer that throws ends its reduceInto'.

options.label: reduceInto keeps v1's sink-only end
options.consequence: On Dart the events pipeline of an ended reduceInto keeps running, the platform-dependent stopping point Spec §10.2 principle 5 removes; the reduce-chain case cannot be written.

chosen: One write chain per reduceInto
why: The Specification itself reads reduceInto as a write of a scan (Appendix A.1 'Reducer topology'), and the write chain is defined by the write declaration (Appendix A.4), so the reduceInto's events pipeline plus its fold is the chain. v1 already ended a reduceInto on a reducer throw; v2 extends that to cancelling what feeds it. This timestamp is an upper bound reconstructed from file birth times, because date -u was not run at the moment of the decision (see notes_for_orchestrator).

question: When does an error end a write chain: the first error raised anywhere in its pipeline (Spec §10.2 principle 5's 'The first error in a write chain ends that chain', read literally) or the first error that reaches its sink unrecovered?

options.label: The first error that reaches the sink unrecovered
options.consequence: A catchError on the error's path keeps the chain alive; v1's 'reaches a sink' criterion stays; matches principle 2 (authors apply catchError to prevent termination; a chain terminates 'due to an unhandled exception') and the intake's L3 'first unhandled error'.

options.label: Any error raised in the chain
options.consequence: catchError could never keep a chain alive, contradicting principle 2 and Guide §4's fallback-state use; v1 G26's catchError clause and every catchError case would break.

chosen: The first error that reaches the sink unrecovered
why: Read as a whole, Spec §10.2 says an unhandled error ends the chain (principle 2) and gives catchError as the means to prevent it, so principle 5's 'first error' means the first one nothing on the path recovers. No Specification change is needed for that reading. This timestamp is an upper bound reconstructed from file birth times, because date -u was not run at the moment of the decision (see notes_for_orchestrator).

question: A stage that several sinks reach: which write chains does it belong to, and what does ending one of them cancel?

options.label: Every chain it feeds; cancel only what feeds no other live chain
options.consequence: Reference-counting semantics, as an Rx engine's shared pipeline has: the shared stage keeps running once per value for the live chain (G27), and an error raised in it ends every chain it reaches unrecovered while a chain whose catchError recovers it goes on.

options.label: Ending a chain cancels every stage of it, shared ones included
options.consequence: Stops chains that are still live, contradicting Spec §10.2 principle 5's 'the topology's other write chains keep running'; seeded as a defect it fails four G26 cases.

options.label: A shared stage belongs to the first sink's chain only
options.consequence: Ownership by declaration order: ending that chain stops a stage a live chain needs, or ending another leaves the shared stage's error ending chains it never reached; no Specification text supports it.

chosen: Every chain it feeds; cancel only what feeds no other live chain

question: Writers before readers: how does start() settle a writer's first emission before a reader connects (Spec §3.13 step 1: 'each topology's first emission sees inputs that their writers have already settled')?

options.label: Synchronously within start(), from the bus's own queue
options.consequence: start() connects each bootstrap activation in the connection order and, before the next connects, delivers the publishes its connection causes and those their deliveries cause; start() still delivers the queue before it returns, as v1's G34 did, so consumer tests that assert right after start() keep working; a self-reference that never settles keeps start() from returning, as it would keep the reentrant drain from ending after start().

options.label: Sequence the connections through provider-zone microtasks
options.consequence: Each next connection waits for the zone's microtasks; the bus cannot drain the zone's queue in production, a microtask a delivery schedules lands after the next connection, and the queue is delivered after start() returns, which every consumer suite that asserts right after start() would notice.

options.label: Connect every activation, then deliver the connections' publishes
options.consequence: What the minimal barrier of topology-dsl-write-chain does: a reader activated before its writer first sees its input's initial value, then the settled one (probe P2: y=0 then y=20), the flicker Guide §6.1 describes and Spec §3.13 forbids.

chosen: Synchronously within start(), from the bus's own queue
why: It is the only option that meets Spec §3.13 step 1 exactly while keeping 'start() delivers the queue before it returns'. The publishes a connection causes are the bus's own (they pass through its publish path), so the bus can deliver them without touching the zone's microtask queue, on the production provider as on a TestBus. 'Settled' covers what a writer emits synchronously from its reads' first values; a value it emits from a timer or asynchronous work reaches readers later, which G34 states. Measured: probe P2 and the G34 settled-writer case pass only on the v2 runtime; the seeded defect that defers the connection's publishes to a microtask fails four G34 cases.
evidence: hsdd/contract/fixture/bus-api/behavior/bus_api_conformance.dart G34 'start connects a writer before every topology...'

question: When, and in what order relative to the bootstrap topologies, does start() connect the observed subscriptions made during bootstrap, and when do they receive their first values (ADR-003 item 6 as amended: 'within start() or in provider-zone work that start() schedules')?

options.label: After every topology, first values within start()
options.consequence: A state subscriber's first value is the settled one; it receives its first values and then the queue before start() returns, in order; an event a writer publishes while start() connects it reaches no bootstrap subscription, as it reaches no reader connected after it.

options.label: After every topology, first values in the first provider-zone microtask after start()
options.consequence: Mirrors G17's microtask, with the queue buffered behind the replay; tests must flush after start() to see a bootstrap subscriber's values, and the queue reaches topologies and subscriptions at different moments.

options.label: Before the topologies
options.consequence: Event subscribers also see what writers publish while connecting, but a state subscriber first sees the initial value and then the settled one, the order dependence Spec §3.13 removes.

chosen: After every topology, first values within start()
why: A subscription is a reader of its topic, so it connects after the writers, as Spec §3.13 orders topologies; Spec §2.1 'Replay timing' has the bus control when a subscriber receives its first value where the barrier depends on it, so start() delivers it itself. ADR-003 item 6 leaves the timing here. Spec §3.13 step 1 says the bus 'also connects' the subscriptions without ordering them against the topologies, so the order is marked for upstreaming. Signal that would have changed my mind: a consumer fixture that expects a bootstrap subscriber to receive an event a topology publishes while connecting; none does (every other suite replays as before on the v2 runtime but for scope timing and the error zone).

options.label: An error event in place of the value, as Stream.cast
options.consequence: onError receives the TypeError, or without one the listen zone's handler (G18's rule for an unhandled error event); the subscription keeps receiving unless it listened with cancelOnError; consistent with how TopicRemoved reaches a subscription.

options.consequence: S58's proposed sentence; a subscriber with onError never sees the failure, unlike every other Dart stream that converts.

chosen: An error event in place of the value, as Stream.cast
why: A widened subscription is conceptually the subject's stream cast to the reference's type argument, and Dart's own cast delivers a failed cast as an error event (subscriber-error-zone C12, off-type-delivery case 2). question: G41: what does 'an exception raised by the bus's own delivery code is an implementation defect and is not swallowed' (Spec §10.2 principle 5) mean for the conversion of an off-type value at a topology read (v1: skipped, TypeError to the provider zone's handler, nidana.runtime D5)?

options.label: A read-stage error: catchError recovers it, else it ends the write chains it reaches

options.label: A reported skip as in v1

chosen: A read-stage error: catchError recovers it, else it ends the write chains it reaches
why: Spec §10.2 principle 5 names three places an exception can be raised (transformer or operator, observer, shell subscriber); a read stage is part of the pipeline, so its failure is a stage error, and the 'own delivery code' sentence then means genuine runtime defects, which G13 now says the bus does not swallow. topology-dsl@v2's Errors and lineage left this choice to bus-api. question: Name check (Spec §4.3, §3.1): does tracing stay among G7's compared fields, which v0.15.1 lists without it; and how are 'the first use of each declaration' and the name freed by removeTopic stated?

question: Re-activation (Spec §3.9; Guide §6.3 'Name every transformer'): IR equality as in v1 (DEC-167), or IR equality plus == on the plan's functions and seeds?

options.label: IR equality plus == on the plan's functions and seeds
options.consequence: A declaration differing in a scan seed or a closure body throws TopologyConflict; an inline closure or a tear-off on a receiver declare creates is unequal to its own next evaluation, so such a topology cannot be activated twice while active; flutter-binding@v1 Refinement 4's holder counts work only for page topologies with named functions (its fixtures' page topology has none, so they pass); navigation-api's resolver, whose stage functions are tear-offs on receivers its declare creates, conflicts with its own second activation.

options.label: IR equality as in v1
options.consequence: No false conflicts, but two different declarations under one id (another seed, another closure body) silently share the first activation, which Spec §3.9's 'any other observable difference' forbids.

chosen: IR equality plus == on the plan's functions and seeds
why: The Guide states the reason (re-activation compares transformers, a Dart closure equals only itself) and Spec §3.9 asks for a throw on any observable difference; the decision policy decides for the option with a stated reason. Probe P1 settles which functions compare equal: top-level and static tear-offs, tear-offs on one const receiver and const callable objects; not closures, not tear-offs on new receivers even with ==. Supersedes DEC-167.

question: Write chains (Spec §10.2, Appendix A.4): restate G26 and PipelineTerminated per write chain; how are the claims after a chain ends pinned?

options.label: Treat it as a new guarantee id
options.consequence: Gates restricted to G26 would miss the claims case; the meaning of G26 carries over.

chosen: Restate G26 in place, compatible, and pin claims kept with a new case
why: A sink and its write chain are one to one, so v1's per-sink report count equals v2's per-chain count; the upstream cancellation is topology-dsl@v2's and replays through bus_activation_test.dart (49 of 49 on the v2 runtime). S59 left the claims case to this contract.

question: During bootstrap, what does removeTopic do for a topic that an unconnected activation reads or an unconnected subscription observes?

options.label: Refuse without force; forced, end the subscription at once and give the read TopicRemoved when start() connects it
options.consequence: G9's v1 outcome (the chains that read the topic end, the subscription ends) holds before start() too; a new G9 case pins it.

options.label: Let the unconnected read reconnect to the fresh subject at start()
options.consequence: A forced removal would silently not affect a bootstrap topology, unlike the same removal after start().

chosen: Refuse without force; forced, end the subscription at once and give the read TopicRemoved when start() connects it
why: Keeps G9 meaning the same thing whenever it is called. No Specification text covers the case; the seeded defect that lets the read reconnect fails the new case.

question: What becomes of an activation deactivated before start()?

options.label: Never connected; claims released at once (G25)
options.consequence: Deactivation means the same before start() as after; a new G25 case pins it.

options.label: Connected at start() anyway
options.consequence: A topology the bootstrap withdrew would compute once.

question: S60's G34 settles a writer's connection before its readers connect, so an EventTopic event a topology publishes while start() connects it reaches the recorders and observers but no topology or subscription connected after it. Holding only the event sinks would break G14's consecutive-delivery rule for a topology that writes one value to a state sink and an event sink, a rule nothing in v0.15.1 relaxes. The contract states the consequence, so no consumer is surprised. question: What does a NidanaModule mount do when its declaration or its acquire throws (a differing declaration, an acquire before start(), a rejected activation)?

chosen: Rethrow from the mount, holding no reference
why: Every cause is a programming error. ModuleScopeObserver reports only because a throw from a NavigatorObserver callback locks the Navigator (DEC-252), which does not apply to a widget; PageScope rethrows. A case pins that no child is built, and a seeded defect that reports instead fails it.

why: The owner's message says so in as many words, and the v0.15.1 intake read the same instruction the same way (DEC-686). superpowers subagent-driven-development's own stop set (destructive, security-sensitive, outside side effect, a plan so broken every path is a guess) is the same shape, so the two layers agree.

question: In which order do nidana.model's 14 phases run, serially?

options.label: Numeric order, 1 to 14

options.consequence: nidana.model.7 (file and cli sets) serves only nidana.tooling's gates; moving it last brings .8 to .14 forward by one phase, which matters only if the run stops early.

chosen: Numeric order, 1 to 14
why: Both orders finish the same set. Numeric order matches the plan's numbering and its lane note, and the phase graph allows it. The signal that would change it: a reason to expect the run to end before .14, which nothing suggests.
evidence: hsdd/spec/nidana.model.md, Phase Plan and Phase dependency graph

question: The planning run's step preamble names the old machine's path (/Users/mohamad.purbo/...) and planning-only rules. What do implementation subagents get?

options.label: A new preamble for the implementation segment
options.consequence: docs/auto-run/step-preamble.md stays the record of what the planning steps saw; the new file carries this machine's path, the git rules implementers need (they commit, unlike planning steps), and the report shape with step kinds.

options.label: Edit step-preamble.md in place
options.consequence: One file, but the planning steps' prompts would no longer be reproducible from git at HEAD, and the file would mix two protocols.

chosen: A new preamble for the implementation segment
why: The planning preamble is evidence for 1071 decisions; editing it would blur what those steps were told. The implementation segment also needs rules the planning one forbade (implementers commit on the phase branch).

question: What may implementation subagents read?

options.label: The planning run's blindness, with the v0.15.1 files as the only reference architecture
options.consequence: No implementer sees the manual run (which may hold code by now) or HSDD's own development notes; experiments under docs/auto-run/experiments/ stay readable, since the tree cites them and some hold prototype code of the replay tool.

question: How is a phase cut into steps for the ledger?

options.label: Three steps per phase (config, code-plan, implement), two commits each, step ids continuing from S96
options.consequence: One skill invocation per step, as the planning protocol had it; the context and the plan are committed and recorded before any code, so a bad plan is visible on its own. 42 steps for nidana.model.

options.label: One step per phase
options.consequence: Fewer ledger lines, but the context switch, the plan and the code share one artifact commit and one gate, and a context defect is found only after implementation.

chosen: Three steps per phase (config, code-plan, implement), two commits each, step ids continuing from S96
why: Each of the three is a separate skill with its own quality gate (hsdd-config's equality check, the derivative's Plan check, the phase gate), and conventions' Execution setup orders them the same way. Continuing the S numbers keeps run.jsonl and the explorer on one sequence.

question: The decision schema's step enum has only planning steps. How are implementation decisions typed?

options.label: Add config, code-plan and implement to the enum and to ledger.mjs
options.consequence: Implementation decisions are typed by the step that took them, and the judge can calibrate them apart from planning decisions.

options.label: Reuse phase-plan for all of them
options.consequence: No schema change, but plan-time and code-time decisions become indistinguishable in the ledger.

chosen: Add config, code-plan and implement to the enum and to ledger.mjs
why: The intake segment added intake the same way (S56). The enum's description says it aligns with the judge's steps, and code decisions are a different population from planning ones.

question: Which execution method runs each phase's plan: subagent-driven-development or executing-plans?

options.label: subagent-driven-development for every phase
options.consequence: A fresh implementer and a task reviewer per task, and a whole-branch review per phase: the most independent checking the run can buy while nobody watches, at roughly three subagent contexts per task.

options.label: executing-plans in one subagent per phase, then one final review
options.consequence: About a third of the cost; the only independent check before the owner is one final review per phase.

options.label: By tier: SDD for full-review phases, executing-plans for gate-only and spot-check
options.consequence: Saves on the declaration phases (.3 to .5), where the surface and reject replays already check most of the work, but spot-check phases hold real logic (lineage, projection, codec) with no per-task review.

chosen: subagent-driven-development for every phase
why: The owner reviews only after the run, so per-task review is the main defence against a wrong turn that later tasks build on. SDD's batching rule still lets same-shape declaration work go to one implementer. The signal that would change it: task reviews in .3 to .5 finding nothing the replays had not, after which the gate-only phases could move to executing-plans.
evidence: superpowers subagent-driven-development SKILL.md, vs. Executing Plans

question: The planning protocol had the orchestrator run no skill in its own context. Who is SDD's controller?

options.label: The orchestrator
options.consequence: SDD works as designed: the controller dispatches implementers and reviewers. The orchestrator's context carries each phase's plan and the short reports, so it is summarized more often; SDD's progress.md and git make that recoverable.

options.label: One controller subagent per phase
options.consequence: Keeps the orchestrator's context lean, but a subagent cannot dispatch subagents, so the controller would have to implement inline, which is executing-plans under another name.

chosen: The orchestrator
why: SDD's controller role exists to dispatch fresh subagents; only the top-level session can. The hsdd-config and writing-plans steps still run in fresh subagents, so the planning protocol's rule holds for every skill that can run in one.
evidence: superpowers subagent-driven-development SKILL.md, The Task Loop
Agent tool: a fork executes directly and does not re-delegate

question: Which model runs each role? SDD requires the model to be named on every dispatch.

options.label: Opus for plan writing, full-review implementers, fix rounds 4 and 5, final reviews; sonnet for context switches, other implementers, task reviews and re-reviews
options.consequence: The most capable model where design judgement or a whole branch is in play, a strong mid-tier model elsewhere, per SDD's Model Selection.

options.label: Opus everywhere
options.consequence: Simplest and strongest, at several times the cost on mechanical tasks such as transcribing declarations.

options.label: Haiku for transcription tasks
options.consequence: Cheapest, but SDD warns the cheapest models take two to three times the turns on multi-step work; the declaration tasks carry long dartdoc and exact reject codes.

chosen: Opus for plan writing, full-review implementers, fix rounds 4 and 5, final reviews; sonnet for context switches, other implementers, task reviews and re-reviews
why: SDD's Model Selection, with mid-tier as the floor for reviewers and prose-driven implementers. Full-review phases (.1, .2, .6, .7, .12) are the replay tool and the analyses, where a subtle bug misleads every later gate.

question: Where do the phases' commits land?

options.label: Node branch impl/nidana.model from auto/v1-impl-1, a phase branch per phase merged --no-ff, the node branch merged --no-ff into auto/v1-impl-1 at the end
options.consequence: Follows conventions' branch discipline; each phase is one merge commit the owner can review or revert; nothing is pushed.

options.label: Commit everything directly on auto/v1-impl-1
options.consequence: Fewer branch operations, but phases interleave in one line of history and the conventions' per-node integration branch is skipped.

chosen: Node branch impl/nidana.model from auto/v1-impl-1, a phase branch per phase merged --no-ff, the node branch merged --no-ff into auto/v1-impl-1 at the end
why: hsdd/conventions.md: one integration branch per node, phase branches merge into it, node branches merge into the root branch, never squashed. The owner created auto/v1-impl-1 as the run's root branch. Local merges of branches the run itself created are not the shared-branch side effect SDD and finishing-a-development-branch ask about.

question: SDD's setup asks for an isolated workspace through using-git-worktrees. Does each phase get a worktree?

options.label: No worktree; the phase branch in the main checkout
options.consequence: Phases run one at a time, so isolation is the branch; the pub cache, .dart_tool and fvm link stay in one place.

options.label: A worktree per phase
options.consequence: Isolation from the main checkout, at the cost of a fresh pub resolution and analyzer cache per phase and paths that differ from the ones the tools assume.

chosen: No worktree; the phase branch in the main checkout
why: Conventions reserve worktrees for phases that run in parallel; this run is serial. SDD's hard rule is never to implement on main, and no phase does.
evidence: hsdd/conventions.md, Companion skills (using-git-worktrees for phases that run in parallel)

question: Where is each phase's superpowers plan saved?

options.label: docs/superpowers/plans/{phase-id}.md
options.consequence: The path follows from the phase id, so the tools and a resumed orchestrator find it without a search; conventions name plans after their phase.

options.label: docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-{phase-id}.md

chosen: docs/superpowers/plans/{phase-id}.md

question: writing-plans ends by asking the human to review the plan and confirm the execution method. Who takes that hand-off?

options.label: The orchestrator: the derivative's Plan check by script, then SDD's pre-flight scan, with the method fixed in advance
options.consequence: The run keeps going; the plan is checked mechanically for HSDD's constraints and read once by the controller for conflicts between tasks; the owner reviews the committed plan afterwards.

options.label: A separate plan-review subagent before execution
options.consequence: One more independent read per phase, largely duplicating SDD's pre-flight scan and the per-task reviews.

chosen: The orchestrator: the derivative's Plan check by script, then SDD's pre-flight scan, with the method fixed in advance
why: The owner is asleep, and the hand-off's two questions are answered: the method by the decision above, the plan's fitness by the Plan check (hsdd-config says to run it before choosing a method) and SDD's scan of every task pair.

question: finishing-a-development-branch asks which way to integrate a finished branch (merge locally, open a PR, keep, discard). Which, for every phase?

options.label: Merge locally with --no-ff into the node branch, keep the phase branch, push nothing
options.consequence: The next phase builds on the merged result, as its dependencies require; each phase stays one reviewable merge.

options.label: Keep each branch unmerged for the owner
options.consequence: Later phases depend on earlier ones (nidana.model.2 needs .1's tool), so the run could not continue past the first phase.

chosen: Merge locally with --no-ff into the node branch, keep the phase branch, push nothing
why: Every phase after the first depends on an earlier one; conventions forbid squash merges of multi-phase work. Pushing is an outside side effect the owner did not ask for.

question: The verification doc's Sign-off belongs to a human reviewer, and the review gate is not passed while an item lacks a disposition. What does the run do with Sign-off, and does it wait for it before the next phase?

options.label: Leave Sign-off empty for the owner and continue once the gate passes and the final review is closed
options.consequence: Each phase is merged with its evidence but without the human review its tier asks for; the owner signs off afterwards, in the tier's depth, and a phase they reject is reworked on top of the later ones.

options.label: Have the final reviewer subagent fill Sign-off
options.consequence: Every gate condition reads as passed, but a subagent's sign-off would claim a human review that never happened.

chosen: Leave Sign-off empty for the owner and continue once the gate passes and the final review is closed
why: hsdd-config's constraint 5 leaves Sign-off for a human reviewer; filling it would misstate who reviewed. The run's own reviews (per task and per branch) are recorded in the SDD flow and in this ledger, and every Outstanding item and Learning still gets the run's proposed disposition for the owner to confirm.

question: When a phase finds a contract gap (a fixture that fails against an implementation matching the Interface), what does the run do?

options.label: Pause the phase, insert an hsdd-contract step (and hsdd-reconcile when phase ids or a Delivery paragraph move), re-run the switch, resume; decide breaking fixes as the owner's stand-in
options.consequence: Governance changes only through its owning skill, as ADR-001 item 8 and the phase context's Discipline require; each fix is a recorded step the owner can review.

options.label: Let the implementer adjust the fixture inside the phase
options.consequence: Faster, but a phase would edit hsdd/contract/, which ADR-001 item 8 and every phase context forbid, and the fixture would stop being an independent check.

chosen: Pause the phase, insert an hsdd-contract step (and hsdd-reconcile when phase ids or a Delivery paragraph move), re-run the switch, resume; decide breaking fixes as the owner's stand-in
why: The Discipline section of every phase context says exactly this, with the human doing the renegotiation; under the owner's no-asking instruction the orchestrator stands in for that human and records it.

question: Do the run's prose rules (no em-dash, no "load-bearing") apply to code, dartdoc and commit messages, or only to HSDD artifacts?

options.label: To everything committed
options.consequence: One rule everywhere, checked by impl-gate on every added line; dartdoc copied from the contracts already complies.

options.label: Only to HSDD artifacts and plans
options.consequence: Code comments could drift from the owner's prose rules, and the gate would need to tell text from code.

why: The rules are the owner's prose preferences, not HSDD's; the planning run applied them to every artifact it wrote. A mechanical check on added lines is simple and catches template text such as the verification template's em-dash title.

question: How does the orchestrator check a phase before merging it?

options.label: A script that checks the write set over the phase's commits, the verification doc, the prose rules and the registries, and runs the phase gate from the context file
options.consequence: The same checks every phase, independent of what any subagent reports; a fresh gate run before every merge, as verification-before-completion requires.

options.label: Trust the last task's gate run and the final review
options.consequence: Cheaper, but the gate output would come from a subagent's report, and a fix wave after the final review would go unverified.

chosen: A script that checks the write set over the phase's commits, the verification doc, the prose rules and the registries, and runs the phase gate from the context file

question: Which calendar date goes in the stamp's `date` field ('Date: today, YYYY-MM-DD'): the UTC date or the machine's local date? The two differ at the moment of the run (UTC 2026-10-26T17:01Z, local WIB 2026-10-27 00:01).

options.label: UTC date
options.consequence: The stamp reads 2026-10-26, consistent with the `date -u` timestamps every report and ledger line carries.

options.label: Local date
options.consequence: The stamp reads 2026-10-27, which is the owner's calendar day but disagrees with every UTC timestamp written in the same step.

chosen: UTC date

A rule that governance dates are the owner's local calendar day would have changed my mind.

question: Which ADRs enter the Decisions section? The phase names Governed by [ADR-001, ADR-002]; the node names [ADR-001, ADR-002, ADR-003]; nidana.model.1 consumes and produces no contract.

options.label: ADR-001, ADR-002 and ADR-003

question: Does the context get an Open questions section? ADR-001 Decision cites OQ8 and ADR-002 Decision cites OQ9, OQ12, OQ-T2 and OQ-F1; the phase block and its (absent) contracts cite none.

options.label: Omit the section
options.consequence: Follows the selection rule literally: only ids the phase or its contracts cite. The five OQ ids stay visible only as the ADR text's own citations.

why: The skill says 'Open questions: only the ids the phase or its contracts cite ... Omit the section when there are none.' The phase block has no OQ id and there are no contracts. Root OQ8, OQ9 and OQ12 are resolved by the ADRs whose text is inline; OQ-T2 and OQ-F1 belong to other nodes.

question: The node's Owns value is a nested bullet list, but the template line is `- Owns: {Owns, verbatim}`. How is a multi-line value laid out?

why: Rule 1 forbids sentences of my own, and the source bullets already sit at the nesting depth the template line implies. Copying them unchanged keeps every character verbatim; the equality check and a line-origin check (every non-template line found in a source file) both pass.

question: The Links line reads `heading "{the phase's heading line as written}"`. Does the quoted heading keep its `### ` marker?

options.label: Keep the marker
options.consequence: The quote is the line exactly as written in the spec, searchable with a plain grep of the line.

options.label: Drop the marker
options.consequence: Shorter, but no longer 'the heading line as written'.

why: The template says 'heading line as written', and the line as written starts with `### `. Low stakes: the link is for provenance only.

question: Does the derivative have a constraint 9 (a tech skill for Dart)? hsdd/conventions.md says no Dart tech skill is installed; CLAUDE.md names none.

question: The self-contained gate (Rule 2: 'Every contract, ADR and OQ id the file names has its text inline in its section. Other phases' ids appear only in the Phase block's Dependencies and Collides with lines') flags ids that occur only inside verbatim excerpts: 8 contract ids (bus-api@v2, flutter-binding@v2, navigation-api@v1, nidana-checks@v1, topic-codegen@v1, topic-model@v1, topology-dsl@v2, topology-ir@v1), 5 OQ ids (OQ8, OQ9, OQ12, OQ-T2, OQ-F1) and 7 other-phase ids (nidana.flutter.1, nidana.model.2 to .7 outside Dependencies and Collides with). How does the rule apply?

options.label: Apply the gate to ids the file selects; excerpt-internal citations stay as the source's words
options.consequence: ADR-001 and ADR-002, the only ids at structural positions (Governed by, Decisions headings, Links), are inline. The flagged ids stay inside the excerpts that cite them, unchanged and uninlined; the file carries no contract section because the phase consumes and produces none.

options.label: Inline every cited contract and OQ
options.consequence: Pulls eight contracts and five OQ rows the phase neither consumes, produces nor cites, contradicting the Contracts and Open questions selection rules and the 'too large signals a phase that touches too much' rule.

options.label: Paraphrase or drop the excerpt text that carries the ids
options.consequence: Passes a literal gate but breaks Rule 1 (no summary, no dropped line) and the task's explicit instruction.

options.label: Stop and ask
options.consequence: Ends the step; the task has already told me to decide and record this case.

chosen: Apply the gate to ids the file selects; excerpt-internal citations stay as the source's words
why: The skill's own selection rules (Contracts: only those the phase's Consumes or Produces names; Open questions: only those the phase or its contracts cite) and Rule 1 (verbatim, no truncation) cannot all hold under a reading of Rule 2 that counts every id inside a mandated excerpt, because the node's Owns and Isolation strategy fields and the ADR Decision text name contracts and phases the phase has nothing to do with. The check script (scratchpad, not a repo file) classified every occurrence by region: the structural positions hold ADR-001 and ADR-002 only, both inline. Rule 2's other-phase clause is violated by the same kind of text, including the phase's own verbatim Scope (nidana.flutter.1). A skill wording that scoped Rule 2 to selected ids, or told the writer to inline cited contracts, would have changed my mind.

question: How is packages/nidana_contract_check laid out under lib/src/, and does this phase add a public library?

question: How does the request parser report usage errors, and which inputs are usage errors?

question: What is 'one line per fixture' for the structure set, and what does a line look like?

options.consequence: PASS|FAIL {set} {path}, with ': {rule} ({detail}); ...' on a failure; subjects are the contract text, the fixture directory and each Dart library under surface/, reject/, behavior/; an unlisted entry, an absent binding or an invocation directory gets its own FAIL line; problems at one path share its line; a final '{n} fixtures: {p} passed, {f} failed' summary; ERROR lines go to stderr. 102 lines over the nine contracts.

options.consequence: cannot name the fixture at fault, which the phase Verification asks for
